sections.overview: The emperor penguin is the largest living penguin, a flightless seabird that breeds through the Antarctic winter. Adults combine a large store of body fat with dense, layered feathers and heat-conserving circulation. When cold and wind intensify, birds gather in compact groups; this social thermoregulation complements their physical insulation and helps breeding males endure long fasts.
sections.identification: Adults stand about 115 centimetres tall and may weigh up to 40 kilograms at the start of breeding. Their mass changes substantially through fasting and breeding. The adult has a black head and back, a white breast and belly, and a broad pale-yellow patch along each side of the neck; juveniles have a duller patch. The similar king penguin is smaller, with a narrower, darker orange neck patch; in an emperor, the pale patch extends down to the waterline when it swims.
sections.habitat: Breeding colonies lie around the Antarctic coast. Most occupy fast ice, frozen seawater attached to the continent; unlike many birds, emperors have no fixed nests and colonies can shift during winter storms. Nearby open-water polynyas give adults access to feeding areas even when sea ice is extensive; local ice conditions shape each colony’s position and timing.
sections.diet: At sea, emperor penguins pursue prey underwater, commonly diving 150–250 metres for three to six minutes, although much deeper and longer dives have been recorded. They eat fish, krill, other crustaceans and squid. In stomach samples from adults provisioning chicks at Amanda Bay in 1986, fish made up nearly all the measured diet, chiefly Antarctic silverfish. That result describes one colony and season: prey proportions vary among sites and years as local ocean conditions alter what is available. Adults can warm small, cold prey internally; breeding birds also return with stomach contents to feed their chicks.
sections.behavior: Colonies are crowded but not defended as individual territories. During severe winter weather, males carrying eggs close ranks to conserve heat while continuing to incubate. At one observed colony, tightly packed huddles remained mostly still, then all birds took small coordinated steps every 30–60 seconds, passing a movement wave through the group. Courtship uses calls. Returning mates locate one another by voice in the noisy crowd.
sections.reproduction: The annual cycle begins as autumn sea ice thickens and adults return to colonies, usually around April. A pair lays one egg, which the female transfers to the male before leaving to feed at sea. The male balances the egg on his feet beneath a brood pouch. He incubates without feeding for 65–75 days, while his breeding-season fast, which begins before incubation, can last about four months. The female returns with food around hatching, and the parents exchange care and foraging shifts. If the chick hatches first, the fasting male can briefly feed it a secretion from his oesophagus. Newly hatched chicks weigh about 150–200 grams, have sparse down, and cannot yet regulate their temperature. At roughly 50 days they can thermoregulate and begin spending time in groups, or crèches, while adults forage. In early summer, down is replaced by waterproof juvenile feathers; young birds leave for the sea around December or January, with exact timing depending on development and ice.
sections.ecology: Emperor penguins link midwater prey to larger Southern Ocean consumers. In spring samples from three western Ross Sea sites, Antarctic silverfish dominated fish prey and connected zooplankton to seabird predators. Their prey mix is not uniform: fish, crustaceans and squid contribute differently among regions, so penguin foraging reflects the local marine food web. At the Haswell Islands, a study found South Polar Skuas mainly scavenged frozen emperor penguin eggs and chicks; researchers judged their effect on emperor breeding success there negligible.
sections.conservation: The IUCN assessment dated 26 February 2026 assigns category Endangered (A3bc). Its climate-dependent models estimate a 45% probability that the global population will decline by more than half by 2073; this is a projection, not a measured future count. On 9 April 2026, BirdLife International announced the move from Near Threatened to Endangered; its summary separately projects a halving by the 2080s. Satellite estimates indicated a loss of about 10% of the population between 2009 and 2018. Early breakup can remove the fast-ice platform before chicks have waterproof feathers. In 2022, researchers judged that four of five Bellingshausen Sea colonies probably suffered total breeding failure after exceptional sea-ice loss; colony abandonment was inferred from satellite images, not observed directly.
